note: Hard travel bounds for raw-count tools. Distinct from the calibrated
range in servo_calibration.json: these say where it is SAFE to drive,
that says where the linear angle mapping is TRUSTED. The safe range is
much wider than the calibrated one, and commanding angles across it
would extrapolate the fit far past its data.
method: Stepped outward from level in 100-count increments until the servo hit
its 0/4095 count limit, with an IMU motion probe and stall guard. All
four directions ended on the count limit rather than a stall, so the
plate may well have been against a mechanical stop before the servo ran
out of numbers -- the guard cannot distinguish 'resting against a stop'
from 'travelling freely' when the servo stops being asked to move.
The 300-count backoff exists for exactly that uncertainty.
consequences: Safe range, level centred:  roll +-7.80 deg, pitch +-8.95 deg.
Full range, level centred:  roll +-9.03 deg, pitch +-10.48 deg.
+-10 deg is reachable only on pitch, and only at full range with level
centred. Roll cannot reach it either way and would need about 11% more
linkage ratio at full range, or 29% within the safe range.
Level is currently 2.40 deg off the midpoint of roll's span and 0.56 deg
off pitch's, so re-centring is worth more than any other single change.
load_evidence: The backoff was applied because a sweep ending on the count limit cannot
prove the plate was still free. The load data says it was: at counts 51,
75, 4025 and 4088 the servos read only 24-28, and the peak anywhere in the
whole full-range sweep was 32 -- about 3% of rated. A plate pressed
against a stop would make the servo push hard and the load climb. It does
not. (These figures are with PRESENT_LOAD decoded on sign bit 10; the
earlier apparent 1000+ readings were a decoding error.)
So the 300-count backoff costs roughly 2.5 deg of span for a risk this
measurement does not show. It is kept as the conservative default, but
the full range is defensible on the evidence.
